title: Kenya Investors Question Sh5 Billion SEZ Investment Threshold
desc: Investors question Kenya's Sh5 billion SEZ threshold, warning it could lock smaller businesses out of long-term licences.
content:
Investors are raising concerns over Kenya's Sh5 billion Special Economic Zones (SEZ) investment threshold, with questions emerging over whether the requirement could make it harder for smaller businesses to access long-term operating licences.

The concerns have renewed attention on Kenya's Special Economic Zones framework, which is designed to attract investment, expand manufacturing and support job creation through designated areas offering a favourable environment for businesses.

Under changes to the SEZ framework, major investments meeting the Sh5 billion threshold can qualify for a special licence with a longer operating period. The provision was intended to give large, capital-intensive projects greater certainty while encouraging significant investments in Kenya.

However, some investors are now questioning whether the high Kenya SEZ investment threshold could create a gap between large corporations and smaller businesses with viable projects but less capital.

The issue is particularly important for local and regional investors seeking opportunities in manufacturing, agro-processing, technology and other sectors targeted under Kenya's industrialisation agenda.

Supporters of the threshold argue that large-scale projects often require substantial capital and longer investment periods before generating returns. They say offering long-term certainty could help Kenya compete for major investments and strengthen the country's position as a regional business hub.

Parliamentary discussions around the Special Economic Zones reforms also indicated that the investment threshold could be reviewed over time, depending on economic conditions and changes in the value of the shilling.

President William Ruto assented to the Special Economic Zones (Amendment) legislation in May 2026 as part of broader efforts to strengthen Kenya's investment environment and widen the range of sectors operating within SEZs.

The reforms are expected to support activities including manufacturing, agro-processing, mining, technology and other strategic industries.

For ordinary Kenyans, the debate over SEZ investment in Kenya goes beyond licensing rules. Major investments can create jobs, increase demand for local suppliers and contribute to economic growth. At the same time, policymakers face pressure to ensure that smaller Kenyan businesses are not left behind as the country seeks large-scale foreign and domestic investment.

The latest concerns over the Sh5 billion threshold could therefore reopen debate on how Kenya balances attracting major investors with creating space for smaller businesses to participate in the country's industrial growth.

As the SEZ reforms continue to take effect, investors and policymakers will be watching closely to see whether the investment requirement remains unchanged or is reviewed to reflect Kenya's changing economic environment.
